content: Breastfeeding involves feeding an infant or young child with breast milk directly from the mother's breasts, rather than using a bottle or other container. Infants possess a natural sucking reflex that allows them to effectively suck and swallow milk. Most mothers are capable of exclusively breastfeeding their infants for the first six months of life without the need for supplemental formula or solid foods. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), alternatives to direct breastfeeding include expressed breast milk from the infant's mother, breast milk from a healthy wet nurse or human milk bank, or breast milk substitutes fed using a cup, which is safer than a bottle and teat. Human breast milk is considered the optimal source of nutrition for infants, as it helps prevent diseases, promotes health, and reduces healthcare costs. However, exceptions exist, such as when the mother is taking certain medications or is infected with tuberculosis or HIV. Experts differ on the ideal duration of breastfeeding to maximize benefits and on the risks associated with artificial formulas. In both developed and developing countries, formula feeding is linked to higher rates of infant mortality due to diarrhea. The WHO recommends exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months and continued breastfeeding for at least two years. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) advises exclusive breastfeeding for six months and continued breastfeeding for at least one year. Exclusive breastfeeding during the first six months provides significant protection against diarrhea and respiratory infections, which are more common in formula-fed infants. Both the WHO and AAP emphasize the importance of breastfeeding for the health of both mother and child. While recognizing the superiority of breastfeeding, regulatory authorities strive to make artificial feeding safer when necessary. Lactation refers to the production, secretion, and ejection of milk, a defining characteristic of mammals. Breast milk is derived from nutrients in the mother's bloodstream and body stores. Studies estimate that exclusively breastfeeding mothers use an additional 400–600 calories per day to produce milk. The composition of breast milk changes based on the duration of nursing, with fat and energy content increasing after the first year to meet the toddler's developmental needs. Research shows that between 12 and 24 months, 448 milliliters of breast milk can provide significant percentages of daily nutritional requirements, including 29% of energy, 76% of folate, 43% of protein, 94% of vitamin B12, 36% of calcium, 60% of vitamin C, and 75% of vitamin A. Breastfeeding offers numerous benefits for infants. Nutrients and antibodies are transferred to the baby, and the maternal bond is strengthened. Studies have shown that breastfeeding may reduce the risk of breast cancer in adult women who were breastfed as infants. Exclusive breastfeeding for at least four months can prevent or delay atopic syndrome in children at risk, though benefits may diminish after this period. Atopic dermatitis, a common form of eczema, can be reduced through exclusive breastfeeding beyond 12 weeks in families with a history of atopy. Breastfeeding while introducing gluten into the diet may reduce the risk of celiac disease, though it is unclear whether this offers lifelong protection or merely delays symptoms. Infants exclusively breastfed are less likely to develop type 1 diabetes compared to those exposed to cow's milk or solid foods earlier. Breastfeeding also appears to protect against type 2 diabetes, partly due to its effects on the child's weight. Breastfeeding reduces the risk of diarrhea-related deaths in infants, regardless of the country's development level. Breast milk contains anti-infective factors such as bile salt-stimulated lipase, lactoferrin, and immunoglobulin A, which protect against infections. Despite being a potential factor in HIV transmission, certain components in breast milk, such as polyunsaturated fatty acids, may reduce the risk of infection in infants of HIV-positive mothers. Breastfeeding does not appear to protect against all allergies. However, babies with a specific variant of the FADS2 gene may have an average IQ seven points higher if breastfed. Necrotizing enterocolitis, a condition primarily affecting premature infants, is significantly less common in exclusively breastfed infants compared to those fed formula. Breast milk contains the ideal ratio of amino acids to support the development of the central and peripheral nervous systems. Breastfeeding for more than eight months has been associated with higher intelligence quotient scores in low-birth-weight children, suggesting long-term cognitive benefits. Breastfeeding reduces the risk of extreme obesity in children aged 39 to 42 months. The protective effect against obesity is consistent across studies and increases with the duration of breastfeeding. Longer breastfeeding duration is associated with fewer middle ear infections (otitis media) in the first two years of life. Breastfeeding also reduces symptoms of upper respiratory tract infections in premature infants up to seven months after hospital discharge. Breastfed infants have improved arousal from sleep, potentially reducing the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). Breastfeeding lowers the risk of urinary tract infections in infants up to seven months postpartum, with the strongest protection immediately after birth. For mothers, breastfeeding is cost-effective and provides optimal nutrition for the child at a minimal nutrient cost to the mother. Frequent and exclusive breastfeeding can delay the return of fertility through lactational amenorrhea, though it is not a reliable form of birth control. Breastfeeding releases beneficial hormones like oxytocin and prolactin, which relax the mother and enhance nurturing feelings. Breastfeeding mothers have a reduced risk of endometrial, breast, and ovarian cancers, as well as osteoporosis. Extended breastfeeding benefits bone remineralization and stabilizes maternal endometriosis. It also reduces the risk of postpartum bleeding and benefits insulin levels in mothers with polycystic ovary syndrome. Breastfeeding difficulties are common but can often be resolved with proper hospital procedures, trained staff, and lactation consultants. Early breastfeeding within the first half-hour after birth is ideal, as the baby's sucking reflex is strongest. Feeding on demand helps maintain milk production and meets the baby's needs for milk and comfort. Proper latching techniques are crucial to avoid pain and ensure effective feeding. Breastfeeding positions vary based on the mother's and baby's comfort, with options including cradle hold, cross-cradle hold, football hold, and lying down. Expressing breast milk is an alternative when direct breastfeeding is not possible. Milk can be expressed manually or with a breast pump and stored for later use. Expressed milk retains high antioxidant activity and can be stored at room temperature, refrigerated, or frozen. Expressing milk helps maintain supply when the mother and baby are apart. Some women exclusively express milk if the baby cannot latch. It is generally advised to delay bottle feeding until the baby is 4–6 weeks old to avoid nipple confusion. Expressed milk can also be donated to others in need.
